title: View from the right
prompt:
Standing to the right of a binary tree, you see only the rightmost node of each level; return those values from the top level to the bottom.

- Nodes have val, left and right (child node or null). In Python they are dicts: node["left"].
- The rightmost node of a level is the last node in that level when read left to right, even if it sits in the root's left subtree.
- 0 to 10,000 nodes; depth at most 500; values are integers between -10^4 and 10^4.
- Return a list with one value per level; [] for an empty tree.
hints: Following right children only is not enough: a deeper level may exist only on the left side.
Traverse level by level (BFS) and look at the last node of each level.
Keep a list for the current level; record level[-1].val, then build the next level from all children, left before right.

solution.py:
def right_side_view(root):
    view = []
    level = [root] if root else []
    while level:
        view.append(level[-1]["val"])
        level = [child for node in level for child in (node["left"], node["right"]) if child]
    return view
solution.explanation: Breadth-first search groups nodes by depth, and adding children left before right keeps each level in left-to-right order, so the last node of each level is the one visible from the right. Every node is processed once.

complexity.notes: w is the widest level. A DFS that visits right children first and records the first node seen at each new depth uses O(h) space instead.

followUps: Return the left-side view and the bottom view (nodes visible from below, by horizontal column) as well.
